title: Secure Software Development Lifecycle
summary: Secure software development lifecycle means building security activities into each phase of how software is planned, written, tested, released and maintained, rather than adding them shortly before a release. It constrains the process and not only the product: requirements must state security and privacy needs, design must record threat models and trust boundaries, code must pass review against secure patterns, and pipelines must run dependency scanning and static analysis before an artefact ships. In a real organisation it shows up as a definition of done that includes security tasks, gating criteria in the build pipeline, and a defined route for handling findings after release. The mistake people make is to equate it with tooling, because buying a scanner and running it late in the pipeline is not a lifecycle approach when the expensive design decisions have already been made and cannot be reversed cheaply.

sources.label: NIST SP 800-218: Secure Software Development Framework

beginner.definition: Secure software development lifecycle means adding security work to every stage of building software. It covers planning, design, coding, testing, release, and later maintenance. Security is not a single check at the end. It becomes part of how the team normally works.
beginner.whyItMatters: Fixing a design flaw late costs far more than fixing it early. Security problems found after release can expose customer data. Teams that leave security to the last step often ship known weaknesses. A lifecycle approach finds issues while they are still cheap to change. It also makes releases more predictable, because the checks are routine.
howItWorks: During planning, the team writes down what must be protected and which rules apply.
During design, they draw the system, mark trust boundaries, and list the likely threats.
During coding, they follow secure patterns and review each other's changes carefully.
In the build pipeline, tools scan dependencies and code, and failures block the release.
Before release, the team confirms that the security tasks in the definition of done are complete.
After release, they watch for new flaws and patch them on a planned schedule.
beginner.example: Think of building a house with a building inspector. The inspector visits when the foundations are dug, when the frame goes up, and when the wiring is installed. Each visit catches problems while they are still cheap to fix. If the inspector came only after the family moved in, every repair would mean breaking walls. A secure lifecycle is that schedule of visits.
takeaways: Security belongs in every phase, not in one check before release.
Threat modelling at design time is cheaper than fixing a flaw later.
Pipeline gates only help if they can actually stop a release.

objectives: Explain what the secure development lifecycle covers and why it is a process control.
Describe the security activities that belong in each phase of development.
Explain why decisions made during design are the cheapest ones to change.
Describe how pipeline gates enforce security checks before release.
Recognise why buying security tools alone does not create a secure lifecycle.
